name: Amittai (Jonah's father)
title: The prophet Jonah's father
summary: Amittai was the father of the prophet Jonah and came from Gath-Hefer in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun in Galilee. He is mentioned in two biblical contexts: in Jonah 1:1, where God calls Jonah to go to Nineveh, and in 2 Kings 14:25, in connection with the prophecy about Israel's border expansion under King Jeroboam II. The name Amittai is derived from the Hebrew word for 'truth' (emet) and can be translated as 'my truth' or 'faithful'. Although Amittai has no independent role in the biblical narratives, he is linked to one of the most well-known stories in the Old Testament through his son Jonah, whom God called to preach repentance to the great city of Nineveh.

versions.summary: Amittai was the father of the prophet Jonah, whom God sent to Nineveh. He is mentioned in the Bible primarily as Jonah's father, and his name means 'my truth' or 'truthful'. Through his son Jonah, he became part of one of the Bible's best-known stories about God's grace toward the Gentiles.

footnotes.text: The name Amittai (Hebrew: אֲמִתַּי, 'Amittay') is derived from the Hebrew word 'emet' (אמת), which means 'truth' or 'faithfulness'. The name can be translated as 'my truth' or 'truthful', and reflects a common Hebrew naming tradition where names express theological confession.

Gath-hefer (Hebrew: גַּת הַחֵפֶר), the hometown of Amittai and Jonah, was a city in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun in Galilee (Josh 19:13). The site is identified with the village of Meshed (el-Meshed), about 5 km northeast of Nazareth. A tradition from the 4th century AD places Jonah's tomb here.

The fact that Amittai was from Gath-hefer in Galilee is remarkable in light of the Pharisees' claim in John 7:52 that 'no prophet comes from Galilee'. Jonah, son of Amittai, was precisely such a Galilean prophet, showing that the claim was historically inaccurate.

According to 2 Kings 14:25, the prophet Jonah son of Amittai served during the reign of King Jeroboam II (c. 793–753 BC). This provides the most important chronological anchor for Amittai's lifetime, which can reasonably be placed in the first half of the 8th century BC.
